content: Scientists have captured the first molecular-resolution images of the ends of rod-shaped bacteria, revealing previously unseen structural features. Scientists have captured the ends of living, rod-shaped bacteria at molecular resolution for the first time, exposing surface structures that were previously impossible to examine in such detail. The images reveal differences in bacterial architecture that could help researchers understand why some species respond to antibiotics differently from others. The breakthrough, led by researchers at UCL (University College London) and published in Nature Communications , relied on an unexpected discovery: bacteria attached to a specially treated glass surface could remain standing upright, allowing scientists to examine their exposed tips, known as poles. To keep bacterial cells from moving during imaging, the researchers coated glass with a chemical that binds to proteins on their surfaces. The technique held the bacteria securely without preventing them from growing or reproducing, overcoming a major obstacle to studying living cells at extremely high resolution. After 20 minutes, the bacteria were generally immobilized horizontally. When left for longer (about 50 minutes), many unexpectedly stood upright, exposing the ends of their cells for direct examination. The team used atomic force microscopy to image these surfaces. Unlike conventional light microscopes, this technology uses a probe just a few nanometers wide that gently taps across the cell, detecting its contours much like a finger reading Braille. The resulting measurements reveal structural details far smaller than those visible with ordinary light microscopy. The images showed that bacterial poles change with cellular activity. Rapidly dividing bacteria (i.e., ones that were dividing rapidly) had fold-like defects at their ends, while less active cells generally displayed smoother, more rounded poles. These irregularities suggest that the bacterial surface may not have fully remodeled after cell division. The researchers also examined E. coli ( Escherichia coli ) alongside Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii , species associated with difficult-to-treat infections. Unlike E. coli , the other two bacteria lacked the network of tiny openings (pores) observed on its surface. These structural differences may influence how the species interact with antibiotics, although their precise effects on drug susceptibility remain to be established. Lead author Dr. Anna Scheeder, based at the London Centre for Nanotechnology at UCL, said: “Our immobilization method opens up exciting new possibilities. We can now study the armor of bacteria across different species more reliably and clearly observe nanoscale differences that were previously difficult to assess.” Bacterial poles are closely connected to cell division, when new ends form as a bacterium splits into two daughter cells. Some antibiotics preferentially act on these regions, making their molecular structure a potential source of information for developing new treatments. Senior author Professor Bart Hoogenboom (London Centre for Nanotechnology at UCL and UCL Physics and Astronomy) said: “Imaging the poles of bacteria is like opening a view of the back of the moon. We are looking at something that no one else has seen before. The poles are where cells divide and so contain critical information about this process. They may also be a particular target for antibiotics, with some bacteria-killing treatments preferring to attack this part of the cell. “Our method of immobilizing the cells without affecting their ability to grow and reproduce also means we can image a much larger range of live bacteria than was previously possible. This is important as it may help us understand differences between species and why antibiotics work for some of them but not others. “Our work is fundamental science that ultimately aims to find new leads to target drug-resistant bacteria.” Reference: “Nanometer-resolution imaging of living bacteria across species and cellular orientations” by Anna Scheeder, Joanna Szczepaniak, Yulianna Koziy, Naomi Mara Claro De Oliveira, William Trewby, Renata Kaminska, Jeremy Brown, Colin Kleanthous and Bart W. Hoogenboom, 9 November 2026, Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78975-y The work was funded by the Wellcome Trust, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), the Rosetrees Trust, and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). The findings have the potential to improve our understanding of how bacteria respond to antibiotics, which is a significant development in the field of science and technology.

content: A changing ocean presents threats that population counts alone may not reveal, and genetic evidence from the Gulf suggests some deep-sea species are already vulnerable. The deep ocean may no longer be the safe haven scientists once believed it was. Hundreds of meters beneath the Gulf’s surface, fish and shrimp are showing genetic warning signs linked to extinction risk, raising concerns that the global biodiversity crisis could threaten even some of the ocean’s most remote inhabitants. A new study led by researchers at Florida International University (FIU) found evidence that five deep-sea species may be less resilient to environmental change than previously assumed. Led by FIU marine scientist Pedro A. Peres of the Bracken-Grissom Lab, the research examined three species of lanternfish and two species of deep-sea shrimp collected between 2011 and 2023. The team analyzed genetic information from 486 specimens to investigate how these populations had changed and whether they could withstand future environmental pressures. According to Peres, the investigation is among only a handful of studies to track changes in the DNA of deep-sea animals over time. All five species showed genetic warning signs associated with increased extinction risk. One lanternfish species, Diaphus dumerilii , had lost approximately 8% of its genetic diversity over just 12 years. That decline was comparable to, or greater than, losses recorded in some threatened and endangered animals over considerably longer periods. The researchers also discovered that all five species had relatively small effective population sizes. This measure does not necessarily reflect how many animals are alive. Instead, it describes how many individuals effectively contribute their genes to future generations. A species can therefore have a large population while relying on a much smaller group to maintain its genetic diversity. “This challenges the idea that deep-sea species are naturally more resilient because they occupy such vast environments,” Peres said. “It shows how much we can miss when we look only at population abundance without considering their genetic diversity and long-term viability.” Genetic diversity helps explain why these findings matter. When individuals within a species carry different genetic traits, their population has more opportunities to adapt as conditions change. Losing that variation can make it harder to survive disease, environmental disturbances, and other threats. Heather Bracken-Grissom, assistant director of the Institute of Environment’s Coastlines and Oceans Division , has spearheaded research into the genetic diversity and resilience of deep-sea species. As a co-author of the new study, she emphasized the consequences of losing that diversity. “Genetic diversity provides the variation populations need to adapt to changing conditions, resist disease and recover from environmental disturbances,” she said. “When that diversity disappears, a species can also lose the ability to withstand future threats.” The genetic findings are especially concerning when considered alongside predictions about the Gulf’s future. Using climate models, the researchers estimated how suitable deep-sea habitats could become for these species by 2050 and 2100. Their projections indicated that four of the five species could experience substantial reductions in suitable habitat, potentially losing as much as 70%. Such losses could place additional pressure on populations already showing signs of limited genetic resilience. The possibility challenges a longstanding assumption that deep-sea animals are naturally protected by their extensive habitats and broad geographic distributions. The findings also raise questions about the lasting consequences of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Earlier research documented substantial declines in deep-sea animal populations following the disaster, although the precise relationship between that event and the genetic patterns identified in the new study remains uncertain. The researchers did not establish that the oil spill caused the genetic changes they observed. Their results instead suggest that some populations may have been vulnerable even before the disaster, potentially making environmental disturbances more consequential. “Our results suggest some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill,” Peres said. “This has important implications for understanding the consequences of environmental disturbances. Events such as oil spills may affect populations that already have limited genetic resilience.” The study, which also included FIU researcher Keith Sellers and Tracey T. Sutton of Nova Southeastern University, points to a gap in how scientists assess the health of marine ecosystems. Traditional surveys can reveal changes in population numbers, yet they may overlook genetic vulnerabilities that affect whether those populations can survive over the long term. By examining DNA across multiple years, researchers can identify threats that might remain hidden in ordinary population counts. Peres believes this approach should become a greater priority as scientists work to understand the pressures facing deep-sea life. “This study serves as a wake-up call for the scientific community,” Peres said, “highlighting the urgent need to integrate genetic monitoring into biodiversity assessments and emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring to better understand and detect changes in marine populations over time.” Reference: “Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling” by Pedro A. Peres, Keith Sellers, Tracey T. Sutton and Heather Bracken-Grissom, 12 November 2026, Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79098-0 This research was funded in part by a grant from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s RESTORE Science Program (ROR – https://ror.org/0042xzm63 ) under awards NA19NOS4510193-T1-01 and NA24NOSX451C0002-T1-01 to Nova Southeastern University, in part by a grant from The Gulf of Mexico Research Initiative (GoMRI), and in part by the NOAA Office of Response and Restoration. title: Data center policy dominated the midterms. The 'Virginia of Europe' is the latest battleground
content: Spain's government is seeking to tighten restrictions on one of Europe's fastest-growing data center booms, as the country's Socialist prime minister prepares to fight an election. Investors like Amazon, Microsoft and Blackstone-backed QTS are on tenterhooks. The measure, which doesn't need parliamentary approval, could be approved by Pedro Sánchez's cabinet by next week, and is widely expected to pass ahead of the Nov. 29 elections. It could potentially cost one of Europe's fastest-growing tech regions billions of dollars in investment. The government first introduced the decree in August, partly in response to concerns over energy demand and prices. After fierce opposition, it put forward a revised version on Oct. 26, but the proposal still includes strict renewable-energy requirements. "These requirements could pose insurmountable barriers and act as an effective moratorium," S&P said in an October report. The proposed rules would require 80% of electricity used by data centers to come from renewable sources matched hour by hour, with projects potentially losing grid access if they fail to comply. Projects already in development or awaiting grid connections would also be subject to the rules, with a five-year transition period to comply. Data center build-out has quickly become a prominent political issue around the world. In the U.S. midterm elections, CBS exit polls found data centers were a major influence for more than half of voters. In Spain, concerns over the water and energy demands of data centers are increasingly part of the election debate as the country faces mounting pressure to expand its electricity grid to meet the demand. CBRE estimates that while developers have announced 10.5 GW of data center capacity across Spain and Portugal, only about 4.5 GW is currently considered realistically deliverable because of grid, permitting and infrastructure constraints. Alberto Nadal, the opposition center-right Popular Party's deputy secretary for the economy, has said a conservative government would repeal the decree. Recent polling shows the Popular Party leading, with several seat projections putting the PP and far-right Vox together above a parliamentary majority. Aragón, a landlocked region in the country's northeast, governed by the Popular Party, has emerged as one of Europe's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs and is at the center of opposition to the draft rules. The region has attracted investors with fast-track permits, abundant renewable energy and land, and international cable connections. Aragón president, Jorge Azcón, wants to turn it into the "Virginia of Europe," referring to the U.S. state with the world's highest density of data center sites. Aragón is set to receive more than 60 billion euros ($66 billion) in data center and digital infrastructure investment over the next decade. But concerns are growing among residents over noise, water use and pressure on the electricity grid. Pilar Alegría, leader of the Socialist Party in Aragón, told a Nov. 15 rally that the election would be decisive for the region's future and for protecting its natural resources. She highlighted the Ebro River, which runs through Aragón, and raised concerns about the resources used by data centers in a region vulnerable to drought. Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, speaking the same day, sought to reassure investors. "It would be a mistake to squander that advantage through poor planning or regulation that creates uncertainty for investors," Feijóo said. Eva Valle, Aragón's economy minister, has also called for the decree to be scrapped. "It is necessary to halt the approval of this decree, which abounds in harmful conditions placed on the sector," she said at an AWS-organized event on Oct. 27, accusing the government of pursuing "a political agenda." Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have said their investment plans in Aragón remain unchanged, while urging Spain to provide long-term legal certainty and regulatory predictability. Google has already put a multibillion-euro data center project on hold pending greater regulatory certainty, according to a report in Spanish newspaper El Mundo , which cited anonymous sources. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. SpainDC, which represents the data-center industry in the country, said the decree would give the group's members the most restrictive data center framework in the European Union and could put 80% to 90% of investment at risk. "We are going to use all the institutional, regulatory and legal avenues at our disposal" to challenge the decree, said SpainDC president Emilio Díaz.
